title: Value at Risk, Explained
objective: Interpret market-risk measures (VaR, expected shortfall) and their limitations.
subject: What does our VaR number mean?
briefing: Treasury reports a one-day 99% VaR of {m:1200000} on our investment portfolio. The board wants to know what that means and whether it's enough.

documents.title: Treasury report
documents.body: One-day 99% VaR: {m:1200000}. Expected shortfall (99%): {m:2100000}. Model uses two years of daily data with no stress period.

options.text: On about 1 day in 100, losses are expected to exceed {m:1200000}, based on recent history.
The maximum we can lose is {m:1200000}.
We lose {m:1200000} every day.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “On about 1 day in 100, losses are expected to exceed {m:1200000}, based on recent history.”

options.text: It averages losses beyond VaR, showing how bad the bad days are.
It doesn't; VaR is enough.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “It averages losses beyond VaR, showing how bad the bad days are.”

steps.prompt: Limitations to flag to the board?

options.text: Two years of calm data may understate stress losses
VaR says nothing about losses beyond the threshold
Liquidity in stress can amplify losses
VaR is illegal

debrief.summary: You explained market-risk measures and their limits.
key_points: VaR is a threshold, not a maximum.
debrief.stronger_approach: Add a stressed VaR using a historical crisis period.
debrief.transfer: The same tail thinking applies to operational and insurance risk.

endings.title: Strong outcome
endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

endings.title: Adequate outcome
endings.text: Solid work with gaps. Your manager asks you to revisit one or two points.

endings.title: Needs rework
endings.text: The work needs another pass. Use the debrief and try again when ready.

title: The Phishing Problem
objective: Design technology-risk metrics and controls for phishing.
subject: Phishing keeps working
briefing: Phishing simulations show 14% of staff click. Training hasn't moved it. What would?

documents.title: Data
documents.body:
- Click rate 14%, report rate 9%.
- Finance team click rate 22%.
- MFA covers 70% of accounts.

steps.prompt: Which metric is the best leading indicator of resilience?

options.text: Report rate (how many staff report the phish), alongside click rate.
options.feedback: Reporting is what lets the security team respond.

options.text: Number of training sessions held.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Report rate (how many staff report the phish), alongside click rate.”

options.text: Click rate only.
options.feedback: A reasonable response, though not the strongest available. A stronger option was: “Report rate (how many staff report the phish), alongside click rate.”

steps.prompt: How do you treat staff who click repeatedly?

options.text: Supportive coaching and stronger technical controls for them; no public shaming.
Name them in a company email.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Supportive coaching and stronger technical controls for them; no public shaming.”

debrief.summary: You shifted from training volume to controls and reporting behaviour.
key_points: Assume some clicks; limit their impact.
Reporting rate is a powerful leading indicator.
debrief.transfer: Behavioural risk metrics apply to safety and fraud too.

title: Permit to Work
objective: Evaluate a high-hazard permit-to-work control and its operating effectiveness.
subject: Is permit to work really working?
briefing: Permit-to-work is our main control for hazardous maintenance. An audit sample suggests some permits are signed after work starts.

steps.prompt: What % of sampled permits were signed before work started?

options.text: Not operating effectively: 15% of permits signed after work began is a serious failure for a high-hazard control.
Effective: most permits are fine.
options.feedback: For high-hazard work, a 15% failure is unacceptable.

steps.prompt: Root cause interviews show supervisors sign late because they cover two sites. Fix?

options.text: Add a second authoriser and digital permits that block work start until signed.
Remind supervisors of the rules.
options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Add a second authoriser and digital permits that block work start until signed.”

debrief.summary: You tested a critical control and fixed the cause, not just the symptom.
debrief.transfer: Critical-control discipline matters in hospitals and aviation too.

title: Insurance Renewal
objective: Design a risk-financing programme: retentions, limits and what insurance cannot cover.
subject: Our premiums are up 30%
briefing: Our property and liability premiums are up 30% at renewal. Brokers suggest raising deductibles. What's the right structure?

steps.prompt: Total expected annual cost of the higher-deductible option (premium + expected retained losses)?

options.text: Higher deductible: lower total expected cost, and a {m:500000} retained loss is easily absorbed.
Very high deductible: cheapest premium.
options.feedback: Total expected cost is higher ({m:3100000}) and a {m:2000000} retention is a big hit.

options.text: Keep current.

steps.prompt: What does insurance not cover well?

options.text: Reputational damage
Regulatory fines (often uninsurable)
Loss of customers after an incident
Fire damage to buildings

debrief.summary: You balanced premium against retained loss and named insurance's limits.
key_points: Retain what you can absorb; transfer what you can't.
debrief.stronger_approach: Model retained losses with Monte Carlo.
debrief.transfer: Risk financing logic applies to captives and self-insurance in any sector.
